one_liner: Header-only C++20 coroutine runtime over io_uring: ~1.22x epoll TCP recv throughput, matches raw liburing, cheaper coroutines than Asio.
what_it_does: Condy is a Linux-only C++20 coroutine runtime built on io_uring. Each `condy::async_*` function wraps the matching `io_uring_prep_*` call and returns an awaitable, so you write `co_await condy::async_recv(fd, condy::buffer(buf), 0)` instead of an epoll readiness loop plus nonblocking recv. It also provides tasks (`co_spawn`, `Task`, `sync_wait`), combinators (`when_all`/`&&`, `when_any`/`||`, and `link`/`>>`, which map to io_uring linked SQEs), a Go-style `Channel`, and wrappers for fixed files, registered buffers, provided-buffer pools, multishot operations (driven by a per-result callback) and zero-copy send/receive. It uses a different programming model from epoll, so it is not a drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: It uses io_uring's completion model: the kernel performs the recv or read and posts a CQE, so there is no readiness notification followed by a separate recv syscall per event, as there is with epoll. Without SQPOLL, SQEs accumulate and go to the kernel in one io_uring_submit_and_wait call per loop iteration, and CQEs are reaped in batches. The ring is created with SINGLE_ISSUER and SUBMIT_ALL and its fd is registered. Each operation's state lives in its awaiter inside the coroutine frame, and the CQE's user_data is a tagged pointer to that state; the README says this removes nearly all heap allocations outside coroutine frames. The run queues are intrusive lists, and wakeups across runtimes use IORING_OP_MSG_RING. Most of the gain comes from exposing io_uring features (multishot recv with provided-buffer rings, fixed files, registered buffers, IOPOLL). Condy matches raw liburing rather than beating it.
when_to_use: Linux TCP servers or proxies where you would otherwise hand-write an epoll loop and want straight-line coroutine code; the published recv test used 16 connections with 64 B to 2 KB messages.
High queue-depth NVMe reads with O_DIRECT, where fixed files, registered buffers and IOPOLL take Condy to raw-liburing IOPS (598K vs 601K for 4 KB random reads at QD 128).

Code that needs io_uring-only features (multishot accept/recv, provided-buffer rings, linked ops, zero-copy tx/rx, uring_cmd for ublk or NVMe passthrough) without hand-rolling liburing state machines.
Thread-per-core designs: one Runtime per core, with Channel and co_switch for handoff between cores.
Task-heavy code where Asio's coroutine overhead shows: 56 ns per spawn vs 373 ns for Asio, about 3.3 ns per switch, and 15x faster channel messaging than Asio in the author's benchmarks.
when_not_to_use: Cross-platform code (macOS, Windows, BSD) or Linux older than 6.0: it is io_uring-only, and the Runtime constructor throws if the ring cannot be created.
If you want a multithreaded, work-stealing executor. Each Runtime is single-threaded, and the author says to start one per core and shard the work yourself.

If you need a long production track record. The project has 22 stars, reached v1.0 in January 2026, and fixed deadlocks in August 2026 (#188 allow_exit+join, #189 CancelRequest) plus a nested-runtime panic (#177).
If you already use raw liburing and are happy with it. Condy only matches it (2610 vs 2560 MB/s multishot recv; 598K vs 601K IOPS), so you would gain ergonomics, not speed.
If you need protocol layers. It is a system-call layer, and the source tree has no HTTP, TLS or DNS support.

integration.form: header-only (CMake INTERFACE target `condy`; optional C++20 module target `condy_module`)
integration.dependencies: liburing >= 2.3. By default CMake downloads liburing 2.15 with FetchContent and links it statically; CONDY_LINK_LIBURING=OFF uses the system copy.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, GCC or Clang. CI builds with GCC 14 and Clang, and pins GCC 14 because of a GCC 15 regression. CMake 3.13+ (the module needs CMake 3.28+ with Ninja and GCC 14+ or Clang 16+). In practice it needs Linux 6.0+, because IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER is always set; no minimum kernel is documented.
integration.platforms: Linux only (io_uring). CI runs on x86-64 Ubuntu runners plus a QEMU x86-64 job on the latest kernel (7.2); other architectures are not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Each Runtime is single-threaded, and run() may only ever be called from one thread (it throws otherwise). co_spawn onto another runtime, Task wait/detach, allow_exit() and Channel (mutex-based) are thread-safe; wakeups across runtimes go through IORING_OP_MSG_RING.

gotchas: The program terminates if a spawned Task is neither awaited nor detached, or if a detached task throws. Internal ring errors call panic_on instead of returning an error.

Runtime::run() does not return when idle unless allow_exit() has been called (sync_wait does this for you). Multishot operations deliver every result except the last to a callback, and only the final result resumes the coroutine.
Kernel/liburing skew: build.md warns that features compiled in from a newer liburing can fail at runtime on an older kernel, and SINGLE_ISSUER (Linux 6.0+) is set unconditionally.
Build: the default configure step downloads and builds liburing, which needs network access and make. The FetchContent snippet in build.md pins tag v1.9, but the newest tag is v1.8 (2026-07-24).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Condy over Asio's io_uring backend when you are Linux-only and want io_uring-specific features (multishot recv, provided-buffer rings, fixed files/buffers, linked SQEs, zero-copy rx/tx) behind C++20 coroutines. Pick it over uring_exec because that stdexec-based library has been effectively archived since 2025. Monoio is the Rust equivalent: Condy's bench puts Condy 1.12x ahead of Monoio on single-shot recv and about even on spawn and switch cost.
verified_claims_summary: On one Ryzen 9 7945HX machine (Linux 7.0, clang 18.1.3, Release build), a loopback TCP recv server pinned to one core with 16 client connections reached 2110 MB/s with Condy single-shot recv at 2048 B messages. That compares with 1734 MB/s for a plain level-triggered epoll+recv server (~1.22x), 1588 MB/s for Asio without io_uring (~1.33x), and near-parity between Condy multishot (2610 MB/s) and raw liburing (2560 MB/s). For 4 KB random O_DIRECT reads at QD 128, Condy reached 345K IOPS vs Monoio's 310K, and 598K with fixed files, registered buffers and IOPOLL, vs 601K for raw liburing and ~200K for libaio.
status_note: Actively developed and MIT-licensed. v1.0 shipped January 2026, v1.8 July 2026, and master is at v1.9 with commits through 2026-09-05, and std::execution support is in open PRs. It is header-only and easy to vendor, but young and lightly adopted (22 stars, one filed issue).
